content: Low-risk tuberculosis (TB) laboratories are defined in the World Health Organization (WHO)’s Tuberculosis Laboratory Biosafety Manual. This classification applies exclusively to tests that are instrument-based. However, this does not imply a recommendation that all tests must be instrument-based. For power requirements, diagnostic systems should be capable of operating on standard electricity and include an uninterrupted power supply (UPS) unit certified for ad hoc use. This UPS should allow the completion of a diagnostic cycle during power outages. Ideally, the UPS should be integrated into the system itself, and the system should also be compatible with battery-operated devices capable of running for at least one day on battery power and being rechargeable. Peripheral centers often face challenges with intermittent power supply, making it essential for manufacturers to provide UPS solutions that ensure sufficient power for completing diagnostic cycles. Preventive maintenance for diagnostic devices should not be required more than once a year, or optimally, once every two years. Maintenance and calibration are critical challenges for devices deployed at peripheral levels, where consistent handling by the same personnel and proper record-keeping are unlikely. Maintenance alerts are necessary to ensure proper functioning, and maintenance procedures should require only simple tools and minimal expertise. Service visits are often impractical in non-urban settings, emphasizing the need for user-friendly maintenance protocols. Data connectivity is crucial for systems implemented in peripheral centers. Mobile phone capacity, which is often available even in remote areas, can be leveraged for data export, quality control, supply-chain management, and surveillance. Data transfer should not rely on high-speed internet and must adapt to the available infrastructure. Exported data should include both raw data and interpreted results to allow re-analysis if interpretation guidelines are updated. Connectivity solutions should be non-proprietary to enable integration with external systems. Cloud-based storage solutions, if used, must comply with local regulations and should not affect instrument functionality if disabled. Electronic components and software should be integrated into the diagnostic instrument. Requiring separate devices like PCs or tablets can limit software updates, as peripheral centers may lack staff with the necessary skills to operate such devices. The operating environment for these systems should accommodate temperatures between +5°C and +40°C with up to 70% humidity, as high temperatures and humidity are common in TB-endemic regions. These conditions pose challenges for transporting reagents and systems, particularly when refrigerated transport cannot be guaranteed. For new products, a shelf life of 12 months is acceptable initially, as evidence for longer shelf lives may not be available at the time of launch. Additional supplies outside the diagnostic kit should not be required, and the system should comply with external quality control standards. Training programs should be developed based on continuing education models to ensure that only properly trained and accredited personnel perform diagnostic assays. Online and remote support systems should be available for retraining, monitoring, evaluation, and refresher training. All training phases must be thoroughly documented. In conclusion, while adopting current WHO-recommended rapid diagnostic tools is essential, it is insufficient to fully achieve universal access to TB diagnostics. Technologies suitable for primary healthcare levels and alternative sample types are critical for progress. WHO has updated target product profiles (TPPs) to guide research and development priorities for TB diagnostics at peripheral healthcare levels. Addressing TB’s global burden requires innovative diagnostic tools that are accessible, affordable, and adaptable to diverse clinical and operational settings. Collaboration, research, and sustained innovation are vital to overcoming challenges and achieving global health goals for TB diagnostics and care.
